result: During perception, orientation decoding in early visual cortex (V1-V3) depends on aperture biases: classifiers trained on one modulator type could only decode the same modulator type (within-modulator decoding) but failed to cross-decode between radial and angular modulators, replicating prior findings.
evaluation: All reviewers accept this replication of aperture bias effects during perception. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'very convincingly show that aperture effects that are present during perception' and notes this replicates Roth et al., 2018. Reviewer 2 confirms 'the data illustrates that working memory decoding is not influenced by the type of aperture, while this is the case in perception.'

result: During working memory maintenance, orientation could be successfully decoded across both modulator types in visual cortex (V1-V3AB), parietal cortex (IPS0/1-3), and frontal cortex (sPCS), indicating that WM representations are immune to the aperture biases present during perception.
evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'very convincingly show that aperture effects that are present during perception, do not appear to be present during the working memory delay.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the data illustrates that working memory decoding is not influenced by the type of aperture' and calls the evidence 'convincing.' The editor summarizes this as 'compelling evidence.'

result: Cross-task decoding from perception to WM in early visual cortex (V1-V3) succeeded only when the aperture bias aligned with carrier orientation (radial modulator), indicating WM representations are only similar to perceptual representations when they happen to align with aperture biases.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. Reviewer 1 notes 'Duan and Curtis also show that when stimulus energy aligns with the carrier orientation, cross-generalization between perception and memory does work (which could explain why perception-to-memory cross decoding also works).' This result is not challenged by any reviewer.

result: Spatial reconstruction analysis revealed line-like representations during WM delay in V1-V3AB and IPS0/1 that matched the carrier orientation (not aperture bias), suggesting oriented gratings are recoded into abstract line-like spatial codes during working memory.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 raises major concerns about alternative explanations, stating 'there seems to be a major possible confound that prohibits strong conclusions about "abstractions" into "line-like" representation, which is spatial attention.' They argue 'subjects could be using spatial attention' and note 'many other stimuli might too' produce similar patterns, identifying an 'inherent inverse problem.' After revision, Reviewer 1 maintains 'this does not entirely address my concern about attention to endpoints' and states 'the assumption that attention can be used in the same manner as a physical stimulus to calculate stimulus energy is questionable.'

result: During perception, spatial reconstruction revealed line-like patterns in early visual cortex (V1-V2) that aligned with aperture bias rather than carrier orientation, with the angular modulator producing patterns orthogonal to the carrier.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as consistent with aperture bias effects. Reviewer 1 notes this confirms 'differences between perception and memory.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges the authors 'illustrate that perceptual and working memory representations do not share a similar representational structure.' No reviewer challenges the perception task spatial reconstruction results.

result: Computational V1 model simulations showed that modulated gratings produce line-like patterns aligned to aperture bias, while simulated line stimuli produce patterns matching WM delay activity, suggesting people store simplified abstractions of the physical stimulus.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 expresses concern that 'many other stimuli might too' produce similar model outputs and notes 'there may be an inherent inverse problem (with multiple stimuli that can lead to the same visual field model).' Reviewer 2 raises a methodological concern that 'the description of the image computable V1 model remains incomplete,' specifically lacking information about 'whether the implemented pyramid also included two quadrature phase pairs.' These concerns about model specification and uniqueness of interpretation remain unresolved.

result: The authors conclude that neural representations of percepts are distinct from memory representations even in early visual cortex, that WM representations are reformatted abstractions of percepts, and that these findings necessitate revisions to the sensory recruitment hypothesis.
evaluation: The editor notes 'more work is needed to establish more generally that visual working memories are abstractions of percepts.' Reviewer 1 strongly objects to the broad conclusions, stating after revision: 'I strongly believe we should refrain from making hyperbolic claims that might preemptively imply all visual working memories are abstractions of percepts' and argues 'a more correct (but admittedly, less "sexy") conclusion may be "Visual working memories of orientation can be abstracted into a line in early visual cortex."' Reviewer 1 emphasizes this work 'uses a specific case: spatial stimuli (gratings) with the task to remember orientation' which 'limits possible conclusions' and notes 'the results may be entirely about the task/cognitive state, and not about how perceptual information is abstracted into memory.'

result: The manuscript frames orientation decoding during perception as driven primarily by coarse-scale biases (aperture effects and topographic inhomogeneities) rather than fine-scale columnar sampling of orientation-tuned neurons.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 challenges the theoretical framing, stating 'The introduction proposes that decoding of orientation information during perception does not reflect orientation selectivity, and it is instead driven by coarse scale biases. This is an overstatement. Recent work shows that orientation decoding is indeed influenced by coarse biases, but also reflects orientation selectivity (Roth, Kay & Merriam, 2022).' This concern persists after revision.

result: Eye-tracking analysis showed that 97-98% of eye positions during the WM delay were within 2° of fixation, and circular correlation between target orientation and eye position polar angle was not significant, indicating eye movements could not account for the findings.
evaluation: No reviewer challenges the eye-tracking control analysis. While Reviewer 1 raises concerns about spatial attention as a confound, they do not dispute the eye-tracking data itself. The data is presented as a methodological control and is accepted as such.
